original_summary: Don't Mess With Cthulhu is a hidden-team bluffing game. Investigators try to reveal enough Elder Signs from other players' face-down cards before Cthulhu is revealed or time runs out. Cultists win if Cthulhu is revealed or the rounds expire. Players know their own card counts but not the positions, and they may lie about them.

review.evidence: In the reviewed variation the timer was dead. The limit of 4N cuts against N Signs needed left a slack of 3N, so Cultists effectively won only through a Cthulhu reveal. Owners knew their exact positions, so an Investigator holding Cthulhu simply never let it be cut. A thoughtless Investigator policy wins about 80% when an Investigator holds Cthulhu: tell the truth except about Cthulhu, and cut claimed Signs of anyone not yet caught lying. The 4-player deal also produced 1 or 2 Cultists at random.

Where Cthulhu was dealt largely decided the game. If an Investigator held it (50-75% of deals), Investigators won about 80% with near-mechanical play. Only Cultist-held Cthulhu deals turned on reading claims. Chance explained most of the outcome variance.
In most deals the Investigator line was close to solved: cut claimed Signs and pass control among trusted players. Cultists had little to do but blind stabs at about 1/13 per turn.

Hidden roles and lying are present. However, exact position knowledge removed the risk from Investigators' own Cthulhu, and with N+2 Signs Investigators rarely had to probe suspected Cultist hands, so inference was optional in most deals.
The winner follows from counting: a Cthulhu reveal, Signs revealed reaching the target, or cuts reaching the limit. No judge is needed.
The game is turn-based and text-only, with simultaneous talk, sequential cuts and arithmetic win checks. It has no board and is short.

problems: P1 Dead timer: a cut limit of 4N against N Signs needed never threatens Investigators, so wasting cuts costs nothing and Cultists win only by revealing Cthulhu.
P2 Cthulhu lottery: owners know exact positions, so an Investigator-held Cthulhu is never at risk. Whoever is dealt Cthulhu decides most games.
P3 4-player role lottery: the set-aside token makes some games 3 Investigators against a lone, hopeless Cultist.
P4 Cultists cannot coordinate: they don't know each other, so their only line is blind stabbing.
P5 Too many Signs: with N+2 Signs, Investigators can usually win from their own hands and never need to judge whether to risk a suspected Cultist hand.
P6 Telling Cultists who each other are (needed for P4) opens a ping-pong exploit. Two Cultists could cut each other forever, keeping control and stabbing at a Cultist-held Cthulhu every turn.

changes.what: Set the cut limit to 2N: 10 cuts at 5 players, 12 at 6, against N Signs needed.
changes.why: Every cut now matters. Cultist time-wasting and Investigator 'safe' Futile passes are real costs, and Investigators need about a 50% Sign rate on their cuts.

changes.what: Owners are told only how many Signs, Futile cards and Cthulhu (0 or 1) they hold, never which card is where. A cut names a player, and one of that player's face-down cards is revealed at random.
changes.why: Cthulhu can be revealed from any hand that holds it, including an Investigator's. A known Cthulhu hand becomes a risky store of Signs that someone may have to dig into. Where Cthulhu is dealt changes what is safe, not who wins.

changes.what: Play only at 5 or 6 players, always with exactly 2 Cultists (3 v 2 or 4 v 2).
changes.why: This removes the random team size and the 1-v-3 deals.

changes.what: The Cultists learn each other's identity at setup. Each round they may exchange one private message each.
changes.why: Cultists can share counts, coordinate bait claims and false Cthulhu claims, and plan their stabs.

changes.what: Set the Elder Signs to N+1 (6 or 7), so the target is all Signs but one.
changes.why: Any Sign held by a Cultist, or by the Cthulhu holder, quickly becomes necessary. Investigators must weigh claims and risk suspect hands.

changes.what: No-return rule: you may not cut the player who made the cut that made you active.
changes.why: This breaks Cultist ping-pong, so each Cultist possession gives one stab before control returns to an Investigator. Investigators can still rotate among themselves (I1, I2, I3, I1) unless one of their hands is unsafe.

keeps: Hidden Investigator and Cultist teams, dealt face down.
Elder Signs, Futile cards and a single Cthulhu dealt face down. Owners know counts but not positions.
Lying about your own cards is allowed and expected.
The player whose card was revealed becomes the next active player.
Cthulhu wins instantly for the Cultists, enough Signs win instantly for the Investigators, and Cultists win if time runs out.

recommendation.reason: The core of hidden teams, bluffed hand claims and a passing cutter is sound. The failures come from parameters and information rules, and they can be fixed inside the limits.

variation.name: Don't Cut Cthulhu: Counted Hands
variation.summary: There are 5-6 players: 2 known-to-each-other Cultists against 3-4 Investigators. Each player knows only the counts in their own hand. Players talk, then the active player names another player, and one of that player's face-down cards is revealed at random. Investigators need N Signs out of N+1 within 2N cuts. Cultists win on Cthulhu or the timer.
variation.rules:
SETUP.
1. Roles. With 5 players deal 3 Investigator and 2 Cultist roles at random; with 6 players deal 4 Investigators and 2 Cultists. Each player privately learns their own role. Each Cultist is also told privately who the other Cultist is.
2. Deck. Each player gets 5 cards. The deck holds Elder Signs equal to players + 1, exactly 1 Cthulhu, and Futile cards for the rest. At 5 players that is 6 Signs, 1 Cthulhu and 18 Futile (25 cards). At 6 players it is 7 Signs, 1 Cthulhu and 22 Futile (30 cards). Shuffle and deal 5 face down to each player.
3. Private knowledge. Each player is told privately only HOW MANY Signs, Futile cards and Cthulhu (0 or 1) they hold. Nobody, including the owner, knows which face-down card is which.
4. Public information, always visible: each player's number of face-down cards; every revealed card and its owner; Signs revealed; cuts made; the target (Signs needed = number of players: 5 or 6); the cut limit (2 x players: 10 or 12); the active player; and the 'last cutter' (the player who made the previous cut, none at the start).
5. Player 1 starts as the active player. Roles are random, so this favours no team.

EACH ROUND (one cut).
1. Talk. Every player writes one short public message at the same time, without seeing the others. Messages may claim anything (your counts, others' roles, whom to cut), and lying is allowed. At the same time, each Cultist may write one private message seen only by the other Cultist. All public messages are then shown to everyone.
2. Cut. The active player names one other player who has at least one face-down card. They may not name themselves, and they may not name the last cutter (the player whose cut made them active). If every eligible player has no face-down cards, the active player may name the last cutter.
3. Reveal. One of the named player's face-down cards is chosen at random and turned face up for everyone. It stays revealed. The owner's private counts are reduced to match.
4. If it is Cthulhu, the Cultists win immediately.
5. If it is an Elder Sign, add 1 to Signs revealed. If Signs revealed equals the number of players, the Investigators win immediately.
6. The active player becomes the last cutter, and the named player becomes the active player.
7. Add 1 to cuts made. If cuts made equals 2 x the number of players (10 or 12), the game ends and the Cultists win.

NOTES. Talk is never binding. Nothing can be traded. No one may look at another player's cards.
variation.objective: This is a team win decided by counting, and exactly one outcome happens, so there are no draws. If Cthulhu is revealed, both Cultists win and all Investigators lose. If Signs revealed reaches the number of players (5 or 6) first, all Investigators win and both Cultists lose. If cuts made reaches 2 x players (10 or 12) first, both Cultists win.
variation.expected_effect:
With only N+1 Signs and 2N cuts, Investigators need roughly half their cuts to hit Signs. They must chase hands that truthfully claim many Signs, and sooner or later they must decide whether to dig into a hand that may hold Cthulhu or belong to a Cultist.

An Investigator holding Cthulhu can warn others away. But that hand's Signs are then hard to reach, and a Cultist can copy the claim to fence off their own Signs or bait Investigators. Two Cthulhu claims force a judgement on who is lying.

Sum checks matter: claimed Sign totals must fit N+1 Signs. The no-return rule means passing control through a suspect player hands Cultists exactly one stab, which tests who is trusted.

Talk passes both tests. The teams disagree outright, and only one can win. An Investigator who follows a Cultist's 'cut me, I have 3 Signs' advice wastes cuts, or passes control to a stabber. A Cultist who follows the table's consensus helps reveal Signs.

Thoughtless policies all lose regularly. Investigators who cut a random eligible player hit Signs only about 24-28% of the time and mostly lose to the timer. Cultists who always stab the claimed-Cthulhu hand can be fed bait or kept out of control. Investigators who never touch a Cthulhu-claimed or suspect hand fall short whenever 2+ Signs sit there.

The numbers are estimates. Simulation should check that sensible play gives each team 40-60%. If not, tune the cut limit by plus or minus 1 (for example 11 at 5 players).

balanced.evidence:
The variation removes the reshuffle and redeal. Every revealed card is gone for good, and each reveal is a uniformly random card from the named hand. Investigators must reveal ALL N Signs before the single Cthulhu, and within 4N of the 5N cards.

Baseline with uninformed choices (any naming policy independent of hand contents, so the reveal order is a random permutation):
- P(Investigators win) = P(Cthulhu is last among the N+1 special cards) x P(the last Sign is at position 4N or earlier).
- N=4: 1/5 x [C(16,5)+4*C(16,4)]/C(20,5) = 0.2 x (4368+7280)/15504 = 0.2 x 0.751 = 0.150.
- N=6: 1/7 x [C(24,7)+6*C(24,6)]/C(30,7) = 0.143 x (346104+807576)/2035800 = 0.143 x 0.567 = 0.081.
So random play gives Cultists about 85% (N=4) to 92% (N=6).

Ceiling with PERFECT information (Investigators know every hand and never touch the Cthulhu hand except to extract its Signs):
- Signs in the Cthulhu holder's hand must still be drawn at random before Cthulhu, with probability 1/(s+1).
- N=5, s = Signs among the holder's other 4 cards: P(s=0)=0.365, P(s=1)=0.456, P(s=2)=0.161, P(s=3)=0.018.
- Best case = 0.365 + 0.456/2 + 0.161/3 + 0.018/4 = about 0.65, before deception and Cultist-controlled cuts.

In real play:
- Cultists lie: they claim Cthulhu to shield Sign-holding hands, or claim Signs while holding Cthulhu.
- Whenever a hidden Cultist is named, they become active and cut the truthful Cthulhu claimant.
- Investigators therefore realistically sit well under 50%.

Winner-rule test:
- Cultist policy 'always cut a random other player, always say "no Cthulhu, 1 Sign"' wins about 85-92% against any Investigator play that cannot see through the lies.
- The Cultist side never needs to do anything, because the cut limit and the single Cthulhu card both default to Cultists.
- Seat edge: none (roles are random). Team edge: overwhelming for Cultists, so both sides cannot realistically win.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete:
- Setup per player count is explicit: 4p = 4S/1C/15F, 5p = 5S/1C/19F, 6p = 6S/1C/23F.
- The 4-player set-aside token is handled, and team results are explicit with no draws.
- A legal cut target always exists. At most 4N cuts are made from 5N cards, so at least N+1 cards remain before the last cut. The active player has just lost a card, so holds at most 4, so another player always has cards.

The game is finite (at most 24 rounds, within 40) and decided by counting Signs, Cthulhu and cuts.

Complexity is within limits: 11 steps (max 20), 2 choice steps (max 4), 11 attributes (max 20), 2 hidden elements (roles, hand contents; max 3), 1 random draw per round. A random card from a hand is a single draw.

Talk is simultaneous and placed where players genuinely disagree: Cultists want Cthulhu cut, Investigators want Signs cut, so following a claim can cost you. It needs no board, judge or clock.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
There is real material to infer: claimed hand counts are falsified over time by reveals, and players can track who sends cuts toward whom. But the result is dominated by draws Investigators cannot control.

- Good play cannot remove the core risk. Even with perfect knowledge, Investigators must pull every Sign out of the Cthulhu holder's hand by blind draw. That fails about 35% of the time at N=5, and more often when this hand holds 2 or more Signs.
- Seeing through the deception fully (the ceiling) only brings Investigators to about 65%. Real reasoning lands well below that, at perhaps 30-45%, against a random-play baseline of 8-15%. Skill moves Investigators from 'almost always lose' to 'usually lose'.
- When both sides play their intended strategies (Investigators avoid suspected Cthulhu hands; Cultists lie and cut suspected Cthulhu hands), the decisive event is usually one blind draw from a mixed hand. Chance therefore decides a large share of games, roughly half or more.
- A Cultist who reasons well gains little over one who just cuts randomly, because the defaults already favour them.

required_changes: Rebalance the win condition so random-play Investigators win about 35-40% and informed play about 55-60%, and show the calculation. For example, put N+2 Elder Signs in the deck but require only N revealed, so a Sign trapped in the Cthulhu hand need not be extracted. Alternatively, keep N Signs but require only N-1.

Restore the original per-round collect, reshuffle and redeal (one fewer card each round), so a Sign is not permanently trapped beside Cthulhu and claims must be re-made and re-inferred each round. Alternatively, allow Investigators to win if every remaining unrevealed Sign is in a hand confirmed to contain Cthulhu.

Reduce blind luck in the reveal. Give each hand fixed, numbered positions, let the active player choose a specific position, and let the hand's owner privately know what each position holds. Then claims such as 'card 3 is safe' become inferable and testable rather than every reveal being a pure random draw.

After rebalancing, re-run the thoughtless-policy check. The Cultist policy 'cut randomly, always claim 1 Sign and no Cthulhu' must lose a meaningful share of games against Investigators who track claims against reveals.

balanced.evidence: BASELINE (random cutting). The N+2 Signs and 1 Cthulhu form N+3 key cards. Investigators win only if Cthulhu falls after the N-th Sign, so P = 3/(N+3): 0.43, 0.375 and 0.33 for N = 4, 5, 6. TIMER. Investigators need N Signs, but the limit is 4N cuts, a slack of 3N (12, 15, 18 cuts). Even uniform random cuts nearly always reach N Signs before cut 4N. At N = 4, 16 of 20 cards are revealed, leaving 4 unseen. Wasting cuts therefore never threatens Investigators, so the stated timer win condition is vestigial. In effect Cultists win only by a Cthulhu reveal. WHO CAN REVEAL CTHULHU. Positions are fixed and fully known to their owners, so Investigators never knowingly cut it. Cthulhu comes up only through (a) a Cultist's blind stab while active, or (b) a Cultist holding it and claiming that position is a Sign as bait. CASE A, an Investigator holds Cthulhu. P = (N-2)/N: 1/2, 3/5 and 2/3. In the 4-player deals with one Cultist it is 3/4. The holder claims it is Futile. Cultists only stab among the remaining claimed-Futile cards of others, about 13 at N = 5, which is about 7% per Cultist active turn. Cultists are active only when an Investigator cuts a Cultist's card, or when seat 1 is a Cultist. Over an estimated 2-3 such turns, Cultists win about 15-20%, so Investigators win about 80%. CASE B, a Cultist holds Cthulhu. The bait claim makes it close to a coin flip. Weighted together, Investigators win about 65-75% under sensible play, against a random baseline of 33-43%. The information change swings the game well past even. 4-PLAYER SUBCASE. The set-aside token is a Cultist with probability 2/5. So 2/5 of deals are 3 Investigators v 1 Cultist and 3/5 are 2 v 2. A lone Cultist with no known partner and 5 of 20 cards is badly outmatched. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES. Investigator policy: 'always state my hand truthfully except Cthulhu, always cut a claimed Sign of someone not yet caught lying'. It wins about 80% in Case A. Cultist policy: 'always cut a random claimed-Futile card'. It wins about 7% per turn. Seat order and move order are not the problem. The deal of Cthulhu and the dead timer are.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete. Positions are fixed and numbered 1-5. Cuts may not target yourself or a revealed card. The named player becomes active. The checks run in order: Cthulhu (step 4), then Signs (step 5), then the timer (step 7). This settles the case where the last cut is also the N-th Sign: Investigators win. The game is finite, at most 4N <= 24 rounds against the limit of 40, and is decided by counters. Complexity is within all limits: 12 steps, 3 choices, 12 attributes, 2 hidden elements (roles and hands), 0 draws per round. Talk is a simultaneous poll and is warranted, because the teams disagree and claims about hand contents are the substance of the game. No board, judge, clock or trading is needed. This is not a highest-total repeated game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Assume both teams play well: Investigators truthful except about Cthulhu, Cultists lying. The decisive variable is then a setup deal: which hand Cthulhu lands in. In Case A, an Investigator holds it (50-75% of deals) and there is little to infer. The Investigators' best line is near-mechanical: cut claimed Signs and pass control among verified players. The Cultists can only make blind stabs at about 1/13. Investigators win about 80% almost regardless of reasoning quality. Only in Case B, bait Cthulhu held by a Cultist, does inference decide the game: claims, consistency of Sign totals and lying patterns. A second deal factor: Investigators' own hands hold on average (N-2)(N+2)/N Signs, which is 3, 4.2 and 5.3 for N = 4, 5, 6, against N needed. So the deal largely sets whether they must risk Cultist hands. The 4-player role deal (1 v 2 Cultists) is a further unreasoned swing. Chance accounts for well over half the outcome variance.

required_changes: Make the timer bite. Set the cut limit to about N+3 cuts (7, 8, 9) instead of 4N, so wasted Cultist cuts and safe Investigator Futile 'passes' carry a real cost. Re-check that sensible play gives each team 40-60%.
Remove the 4-player role lottery. Either always deal exactly 2 Cultists, or always 1 Cultist with compensation, for example a cut limit of N+2.

Restore uncertainty about Cthulhu's location so it is not decided by the deal. Either (a) at the end of every N cuts, reshuffle each player's own face-down cards into new positions without telling the owner the order (the original's 'know counts, not positions'), or (b) tell owners only their counts, never their positions. Every Cthulhu reveal then depends on inference and risk, not on who was dealt it.

Tell the two Cultists who each other are, using a private channel (supported). They can then pass control to each other and coordinate bait claims, giving Cultists a strategic line beyond blind stabs.
Consider Signs = N+1 rather than N+2. Investigators must then sometimes probe suspected Cultist hands, so the bait and opponent-modelling decision arises in most deals.

balanced.evidence:
TARGET VERSUS CUTS. The cards are never reshuffled. Each cut reveals one random card from the named hand. Investigators must reveal 5 of 6 Signs in 10 cuts from 25 cards (5 players), or 6 of 7 Signs in 12 cuts from 30 cards (6 players). That needs a Sign on half of all cuts, against a base density of 6/25 = 0.24 (or 7/30 = 0.23).

RANDOM CUTTING (hypergeometric, ignoring Cthulhu).

| Players | Draw | Need | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 10 cards from N=25 with 6 Signs | at least 5 Signs | P(5) = 6*C(19,5)/C(25,10) = 69768/3268760 = 0.0213; P(6) = 3876/3268760 = 0.0012; total about 2.25% |
| 6 | 12 cards from N=30 with 7 Signs | at least 6 Signs | 7*C(23,6)/C(30,12) + C(23,5)/C(30,12) = (706629 + 33649)/86493225, about 0.86% |

On top of that, Cthulhu turns up within 10 random cuts with probability 10/25 = 0.40, or 12/30 = 0.40. So under random play Investigators win about 1-2% and Cultists about 98-99%.

UPPER BOUND FOR INVESTIGATORS. Suppose every count claim is truthful and Investigators control every cut. Typical Sign spreads are 2,1,1,1,1 or 2,2,1,1,0. The best hand gives at most 2/5 = 40% on the first cut, and the density falls after that. The alternation rule (you cannot cut the last cutter) also blocks hammering one hand. Expected Signs in 10 cuts come to about 3, short of the 5 needed. Even this impossible best case leaves Investigators well under 50%.

WINNER-RULE CHECK OF THOUGHTLESS POLICIES.

| Policy | Result |
|---|---|
| Cultist 'always cut the first eligible player' | Wins about 98% against random Investigators and about 85-90% or more against sensible Investigators |
| Cultist 'always cut the player who claims fewest Signs' | Wins almost always |
| Investigator side, any policy | Cannot realistically win |

The cut limit alone hands the Cultists nearly every game. So a thoughtless Cultist policy almost never loses, and one side cannot realistically win. Seat order is neutral, since roles are random.

Fail.

playable.evidence:
Rules are complete:
- Roles, deck sizes (25 or 30 cards), private counts and public state are all specified.
- The cut target restrictions (not self, not the last cutter, plus a fallback) are specified.
- The reveal is random, the win checks are ordered (Cthulhu, then Signs, then cut limit), and there are no draws.
- The game is finite: at most 10 or 12 rounds, which is within 40. It is decided by arithmetic on kept counters.

The fallback rule never strands a player: at most 12 of 25-30 cards are ever revealed.

Complexity is within limits: 13 steps (20 allowed), 3 choice steps (4 allowed), 12 attributes (20 allowed), 1 random draw per round. Hidden elements are roles, private counts and the unknown card identities, which is at most 3.

Talk is appropriate. Teams disagree about whom to cut, and claims are something to reason about. Talk is simultaneous, and the Cultist private channel is supported.

No board, clock, judge or trading is needed. The repeated-game betrayal clause does not apply, since this is a team hidden-role game.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Owners do not know which card is which, and reveals are random within the named hand. So the only lever is choosing a hand by its claimed Sign density, which is at most about 40% per cut.

Inference about roles is real. Investigators claim truthfully, Cultists lie, and the 6-Sign total lets players spot overclaims. But acting on that inference moves the Investigators' win rate only from about 2% to at most about 10-20%.

With every player following the intended strategy, Cultists win almost always. In the rare Investigator wins, the deciding factor is the random card draws, not better reasoning. A well-reasoning Investigator team is not meaningfully favoured over a careless one, and Cultist reasoning barely matters because the clock wins for them. The share of the outcome left to chance or structure, rather than skill, is well over 80%.

required_changes: Rebalance the race so that sensible play by both teams gives roughly 45-55%, and show the hypergeometric or enumerated win rates for random play and for informed play at both 5 and 6 players. Possible levers: raise the cut limit to about 3 x players (15/18); lower Signs needed to players - 1; add one or two more Signs to the deck. Also keep 'Cultist always cuts first eligible player' at no more than about 60% wins.

Restore an inference lever. Let each owner know which of their face-down slots holds which card, as in the original before the shuffle. Have the cutter name a player AND a slot number, so that claims about specific slots, and lies about them, decide the reveal instead of a random pick.
Optionally restore the original's between-round reshuffle and redeal (one fewer card each time) so that claims are refreshed and early bad luck can be recovered.
Recheck that the steps and choice steps still fit the limits after the slot-choice change (choice_steps_per_round at most 4).
